edits.new: Plant celery outside only after hard frosts are over, because cold young plants often bolt later. Space them 6 to 12 inches apart in rich, damp soil, and harden them off first by watering a little less.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (VH021: 6-12 in)

edits.new: Set celery out only after the danger of hard frost and prolonged cold has passed, since chilled young plants bolt. Space 6 to 12 inches apart in rich, moist soil, and harden off first by easing water, not by chilling.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (VH021: 6-12 in)

edits.new: You do not thin celery, because you plant it as young transplants spaced where they will grow, 6 to 12 inches apart, instead of sowing a crowded row. Planting on the closer side gives more but slimmer stalks; a bit farther apart gives stockier plants. You set the spacing when you plant, so there is nothing to pull out later.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (VH021: 6-12 in)

edits.new: Celery is not thinned, because it is grown from transplants set directly at their final spacing of 6 to 12 inches rather than from a thickly sown row. Closer spacing (toward 6 inches, especially for self-blanching types planted in blocks) gives higher yield but more slender stalks, while wider spacing gives stockier plants; choose your spacing at transplanting rather than thinning later.
edits.reason: restates the moved in-row figure (VH021: 6-12 in)
